newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU budget pact insufficient, German institute says.
newsitem.headline: EU budget pact insufficient, German institute says.

text.p: The stability pact agreed by European Union members last December will probably fail to ensure lasting fiscal discipline after European monetary union, one of Germany's six leading economic institutes said.

The effectiveness of the pact may be impaired by "opportunistic behaviour" by governments, which under the pact have the final say on whether sanctions should be imposed, the Kiel Institute of World Economics said in a report.

In addition, the time span between the occurrence of excessive deficits and the implementation of sanctions was too long, the institute said in a summary of the report released ahead of publication on Monday.
It said an independent commission should be set up to decide on deficits and that sanctions should be imposed in the same year as the excessive deficit occurred.

While the stability pact agreed last December at an EU summit meeting in Dublin made several points of the Maastricht Treaty more precise, "the decisions will probably not suffice to achieve fiscal discipline for several reasons," it said.

The agreement, reached at Germany's insistence, lays down sanctions for countries whose budget deficit exceeds the target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) set by the Maastricht Treaty on European Union.
But the pact allows exceptions if a country's spending is boosted by circumstances beyond its control or if its economy suffers a severe recession.

The institute said several EU states opposed strengthening the sanction mechanism because they feared it would hamper automatic stabilisers -- a process whereby an economic contraction automatically boosts government spending through increased unemployment benefit payouts.

But the institute said its analysis of the cyclical components of budget deficits in EU countries showed that such stabilisers would be effective even if the stability pact were applied very strictly.

"In order to avoid an excessive deficit, it would be necessary to reduce structural deficits considerably, in some cases even to zero. While this is an ambitious target, it is precisely what was decided upon in Dublin," the report said.
